lines.text: You were gone for one year.
Earth was gone for seventy.
And around month seven, the robot flying with you started talking like your little sister.
She was eight when you left.
The docking light turns green. The robot turns to face you.
Someone's waiting at the gate, it says.
But let's go back.
In twenty thirty-one, a company was paying five million dollars for one year in space.
One pilot. One robot. One trip out into deep space, and back.
The catch was in the fine print.
Earth time: about seventy years.
That's not a trick. It's Einstein.
The faster you move, the slower your clock ticks.
GPS satellites have to correct for it every single day, or your map would drift by about ten kilometers.
NASA even measured it on twins. After almost a year in orbit, one came home younger than his brother, by less than a hundredth of a second.
The fastest thing we've ever built reached six hundredths of one percent of light speed.
Your ship does ninety-nine point nine nine percent.
At that speed, one year for you is about seventy for everyone else.
You took the job for your little sister, Mia.
Eight years old. The money would cover everything she'd ever need.
She made you promise to come back. One year, you told her.
She gave you a drawing for the trip. A robot, holding a flower.
Your only company is Otto, a maintenance robot with a screen for a face and zero sense of humor.
For six months, it says exactly three things.
And Earth goes quiet. You're racing away from your own messages at nearly the speed of light.
In six months, barely one day of news catches up with you.
Then you turn around.
And seventy years of Earth come at you in six months.
Every day on board, almost five months of her life arrive.
Mia at twelve, with braces. At eighteen, graduating. At twenty-five, with a company badge.
And Otto starts to change.
It hums the song you used to sing her.
It tells her terrible jokes.
It draws flowers on its own face.
You think deep space is frying its circuits.
Then you open its update log.
Four thousand patches, every one signed by the same engineer.
Mia joined the company at twenty-two. She couldn't fly out to you.
So for fifty years, she sent herself instead. One line of code at a time.
Every joke, every song, every flower was her.
Now the gate opens.
She's seventy-eight. And she's holding a flower.
You promised her one year. You kept it. So did she.
Would you take the job? Tell me in the comments.
